assignments.title: 1.1 Critical Questions: Letters of Columbus
assignments.html:
1. Columbus describes the islanders as having "no iron, nor weapons" and as being remarkably generous, giving freely whatever is asked of them. What does his choice to record these two facts side by side suggest about how he was already imagining future relations between Spain and these peoples, even in this very first report, before any policy had been decided?
  2. Counterfactual: Suppose Columbus had instead landed on the coast of a powerful, densely populated, iron-working state, the kind of civilization he actually believed he was sailing toward in Asia. European sailors who reached Ming China by sea around this same period traded there respectfully, as guests operating at the emperor's pleasure, because China's military and political strength gave them no other choice. How might this letter have read differently if Columbus had found a society with that kind of strength instead of the one he describes? What does the comparison suggest about how much of what followed in the Caribbean was decided by ideas, and how much by a simple imbalance of power?
  3. Columbus repeatedly frames his voyage in religious terms: thanking "Our Lord," naming the first island for "the Divine Majesty," and closing with a promise of "converts to our holy faith." Why might Columbus have needed this letter, addressed to a royal court that had financed his voyage expecting a financial return, to also sound like a religious triumph?
  4. Columbus never uses any word resembling "America," and refers throughout to "the Indies." What does his own vocabulary reveal about the gap between what had actually happened and what its own participants believed was happening? Why does that gap matter when a historian today uses this letter as evidence?

assignments.title: 1.2 Primary Source Exercise: Hariot's Report of Virginia
assignments.html:
Four questions, fixed shape: counterfactual, causation, concept, significance.

  1. Counterfactual. Hariot wrote partly to correct "slanderous" rumors that had discouraged people from investing in or settling the Virginia colony. Suppose those negative rumors had never circulated in the first place. Would a report like this one still have been necessary? Would it have looked any different if Hariot had not been writing against a rival version of events? Explain your reasoning.
  2. Causation. Why does Hariot organize so much of his report around "commodities" (things that could be sold or profitably raised) rather than simply describing the land and its people out of curiosity? What does the structure of the document (his own stated three-part plan) reveal about who he expected to read it and why?
  3. Concept. Hariot describes the Algonquian people as uncertain "whether to think us gods or men" upon seeing English instruments, guns, and books. What does this passage suggest about how a large gap in technology can shape the way two peoples interpret each other on first contact, and how does that compare to what Columbus's letter suggested about Spanish attitudes toward the Taíno's lack of iron weapons?
  4. Significance. Read Columbus's letter (1493) and Hariot's report (1588) as a pair, separated by ninety-five years, two different home countries, and two different landscapes. What has stayed the same about how European explorers described the peoples and resources of the Americas across that span? What, if anything, has changed?

What You're Doing: Numbers on a page (thirty-three days, 2,400 miles believed, 12,000 miles actual) are easy to read past. In this session you will stand at a placed world map and physically trace Columbus's 1492 route leg by leg, marking the two places where the voyage's contingent turning points happened: the Canary Islands stop and the landfall at San Salvador. This is your first VR session of the course, so take your time getting oriented.

How to Join: Device: VR headset (desktop fallback available). VR session ID: HIS7-WK1-A (open to any group size). Environment: Age of Exploration Atlas Room. On arrival, you will spawn facing a large table-mounted world map with a pre-placed whiteboard showing Columbus's 1492 route already marked in outline.

What to Do, In Order:

  1. Read the pre-placed whiteboard at the spawn point. It marks Palos (departure), the Canary Islands (resupply stop), and the open-ocean crossing.
  2. Place a sticky note at the Canary Islands marker explaining, in your own words, why this stop mattered (the westward trade winds).
  3. Place a second sticky note at the San Salvador landfall marker with the date (October 12, 1492) and one sentence on what Columbus believed he had reached.
  4. Record a 60–90 second spatial recording standing at the map, narrating the route in your own words as if explaining it to someone who has never heard the story.

assignments.title: 2.1 Critical Questions: Díaz
assignments.html:
1. Díaz compares Tenochtitlan to "the legend of Amadis," a popular Spanish chivalric romance novel of his day, and says his soldiers wondered if they were dreaming. What does this comparison reveal about the mental categories European soldiers had available for making sense of something genuinely new to them, and how might that frame of reference have shaped what they noticed and what they overlooked?
  2. Counterfactual. Díaz wrote this account roughly fifty years after the events it describes, partly to claim credit for common soldiers that Cortés's own official letters had reserved for himself. Suppose Díaz had instead written his account immediately after 1521, as a young soldier, with no grievance yet against Cortés's version of events. Would you expect this passage to read differently? What, specifically, might change?
  3. Díaz closes by noting that "today all is overthrown and lost, nothing left standing." What historical process does this single sentence compress, and why might an old soldier, looking back, choose to end his description of the city's grandeur with its destruction rather than with the moment of first sight?
  4. This account and Cortés's own official letters (which you'll read next) describe the same campaign from two different positions within it. What kind of disagreement would you expect between a commander's official report to his king and a foot soldier's decades-later memoir, and what kind of agreement, if any, would actually strengthen a historian's confidence in a specific claim?

assignments.html:

Use Heading styles for each of your two numbered responses. Submit your finished .docx by uploading it to this assignment in Canvas.

  1. Cortés spends a striking amount of this letter describing the size, order, and regulation of the Tenochtitlan market, comparing it favorably to Salamanca. Why would emphasizing the market's order, of all things, help Cortés's legal case to the king that his unauthorized expedition deserved royal approval rather than punishment?
  2. Cortés asks the king to "hold me excused if in some things I have exceeded my instructions." What unstated theory of loyalty and service is Cortés appealing to here: one where obedience to explicit orders is the highest duty, or one where a subordinate's outcomes can retroactively justify disobedience? Which theory would a king in Charles V's position have reason to accept or resist, and why? assignments.title: 3.1 Critical Questions: Champlain
assignments.html:
1. Champlain fought this battle to help the Huron and Algonquin against their Iroquois rivals. What does his willingness to take sides in a Native conflict, rather than remain neutral, reveal about how deeply French trade interests were already entangled with Native alliance politics by 1609, well before large-scale French settlement had even begun?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Champlain's arquebus had misfired that day, or the shot had missed. Based on what this week's lesson says about why France needed Native alliance, would France's relationship with the Iroquois and Huron likely have developed very differently over the following decades, or would the underlying dynamics have reasserted themselves regardless of this one battle's outcome?
  3. Champlain reports his allies saying the enemy would "never take courage again against us" after seeing the arquebus's effect. What does this passage suggest about how the introduction of a new weapons technology can reshape the balance of power between rival Native nations, independent of any European power's deliberate policy?
  4. This is Champlain's own account of a battle he personally fought in and takes clear credit for winning. What kind of information should a historian be especially cautious about accepting at face value from this passage, and what kind of information is this source still useful for even given that caution?

assignments.title: 3.2 Primary Source Exercise: The Jesuit Relations
assignments.html:
1. Counterfactual. The missionaries note that Huron sorcerers linked baptism to sickness and death because missionaries often baptized the dying. Suppose Jesuit missionaries had instead only baptized healthy converts and never approached the dying. Would this specific obstacle to conversion likely have been smaller? What different obstacle might have taken its place?
  2. Causation. Why would a Jesuit writing home need to acknowledge failures and resistance rather than simply report unbroken success to his superiors and the French Catholic public funding the mission?
  3. Concept. The missionaries interpret Huron religious specialists (whom they call "sorcerers") as agents of "the Devil." What does this framing reveal about how the missionaries made sense of a belief system genuinely different from their own, and what does it prevent them from seeing about that belief system on its own terms?
  4. Significance. This week you have read a soldier-explorer's battle account (Champlain) and a missionary's report (the Jesuits). Both describe relationships with the same Huron and Iroquois nations. What does each source reveal about French colonization that the other could not have shown on its own?

assignments.title: 4.1 Critical Questions: John Smith
assignments.html:
Tuesday's Assessment: Critical Questions

  1. Smith describes his own work-discipline policy and takes personal credit for the colony's food supply, "without which they had all starved." What does the fact that Smith wrote and published this account himself, defending himself against rivals, suggest you should watch for when reading his description of his own leadership?
  2. Counterfactual. Powhatan offered Smith his daughter, land, and lasting friendship if Smith would stay and leave his weapons behind. Suppose Smith had accepted. Based on what you know about early Jamestown's dependence on Powhatan trade, would this alliance have likely changed the colony's later trajectory toward war, or would English demand for land have produced conflict eventually regardless?
  3. Smith reports that Powhatan's "loves turned into malice" once Smith insisted on leaving. What does this suggest about how personally, rather than institutionally, early Anglo-Powhatan diplomacy operated?

assignments.title: 4.2 Primary Source Exercise: John Smith

  2. Concept. Smith's work-discipline rule and his account of Powhatan's diplomacy both appear in the same short document.   3. Significance. assignments.title: 5.1 Critical Questions: The Mayflower Compact
assignments.html:
1. The signers describe themselves as "loyal subjects" of King James in the same document where they "covenant and combine" themselves into a self-governing "civil body politic." What does holding both of these ideas together suggest about how the colonists understood the relationship between the authority they already had and the authority they were creating?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose the Mayflower had reached its intended destination within the Virginia Company's chartered territory, where an existing colonial government already had legal authority. Would a document like this one have been necessary?
  3. The compact commits the signers to laws made "for the general good of the colony," decided by whatever process the group would establish, rather than laws handed down by a king or company. What concept is at work here that you will see argued much more fully, more than a century and a half later, in the Declaration of Independence?
  4. Only adult men signed the compact, though women, children, and servants were also aboard and subject to whatever government it created. What does this detail reveal about who counted as a full member of the "civil body politic" in 1620?

assignments.html:

  1. Winthrop credits Plymouth's endurance to being "knit together by their own agreement before ever they set foot ashore," that is, to the Mayflower Compact. Suppose Plymouth's colonists had gone ashore in 1620 with no such agreement, each family fending for itself with no shared civil authority. Based on what you know of Plymouth's actual first year, would you expect the colony to have survived at all? Defend your answer.

assignments.title: 6.1 Critical Questions: Bacon's Declaration
assignments.html:
Tuesday's Assessment: Critical Questions

  1. Bacon accuses Berkeley of "monopolizing the trade with the beaver" for "some few" favorites, while ordinary frontier settlers went unprotected from Native attacks. What does pairing an economic grievance with a security grievance in the same document suggest about how Bacon expected to build the broadest possible coalition of support?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Bacon had not died of dysentery in October 1676, shortly after his forces burned Jamestown. Based on what you know about how personally Bacon's followers seem to have rallied around him specifically, do you think the rebellion would have achieved lasting political change in Virginia, or would royal authority have eventually reasserted itself regardless of Bacon's survival?
  3. Bacon declares Berkeley "a traitor to the King and country," not a traitor to the colonists, but to the King. What does this framing reveal about how Bacon needed to present his own armed rebellion in order to avoid it looking like rebellion against royal authority itself?

assignments.title: 6.2 Primary Source Exercise: Bacon's Declaration
assignments.html:
Thursday's Assessment: Primary Source Exercise

  1. One influential historical argument (associated with the historian Edmund Morgan) holds that Virginia's elite, alarmed by seeing poor white frontier settlers and slave and indentured Black and white laborers unite behind Bacon against the colony's governing class, moved afterward to harden the legal distinction between white and Black labor. Explain, in your own words, what this argument claims caused Virginia's shift toward a more rigid slave system, and why it treats Bacon's Rebellion as a turning point rather than a footnote.
  2. Concept. Bacon's Declaration reads much like a legal indictment, listing specific charges against a specific named official. What does this legal, itemized structure suggest about what kind of political change Bacon was actually seeking: a new theory of government, or a change of specific personnel and policies within the existing system?
  3. Significance. Virginia's House of Burgesses, established in 1619, gave at least some colonists a formal, peaceful channel for political grievance decades before Bacon's Rebellion. Why might Bacon's supporters have turned to armed rebellion anyway? What does your answer suggest about the limits of formal political participation when a colony's power is concentrated among a small elite?

assignments.title: 7.1 Critical Questions: Clarkson
assignments.html:
Tuesday's Assessment: Critical Questions

  1. Clarkson anticipates and directly answers an objection: that slavery must be natural and justifiable because it has "existed in almost every age and country of the world." What is his counter-argument, and do you find the analogy he draws to war persuasive? Why or why not?
  2. Clarkson acknowledges that the "enslavement of the Africans by their own countrymen" predated European arrival, but argues this "does not excuse the European for buying" slaves. What moral distinction is Clarkson drawing between the existence of an evil and one's own participation in expanding it?
  3. Concept. Clarkson argues "every man has a right to his own body" that "no sale, no purchase" can transfer without "a fair and open trial." What theory of rights is Clarkson drawing on here, and how does it compare to the Natural Law theory you will encounter later this semester in the Declaration of Independence?

assignments.title: 7.2 Primary Source Exercise: Clarkson
assignments.html:
Thursday's Assessment: Primary Source Exercise

  1. Counterfactual. Suppose Clarkson had written this essay in 1685 instead of 1785, before the Enlightenment natural-rights arguments he draws on were as widely developed. Would an argument like his have been available in the same form?
  2. Colonial slave codes, which hardened over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, increasingly defined slave status as permanent, hereditary through the mother, and attached to race rather than to any specific crime, debt, or captivity in war. How does this legal development directly contradict the standard Clarkson demands in his closing paragraph?
  3. Significance. Slaves resisted their condition throughout the colonial period, including organized revolts such as the 1712 uprising in New York City and the 1739 Stono Rebellion in South Carolina, both of which colonial governments met with harsh reprisals and even stricter slave codes. What does the persistence of resistance, despite severe punishment, suggest about how slaves themselves answered the question Clarkson poses in his essay's title?

assignments.title: 8.1 Critical Questions: Edwards
assignments.html:
1. Edwards distinguishes "speculative or notional" knowledge from a "sense of the heart," comparing it to the difference between rationally knowing honey is sweet and actually tasting its sweetness. What kind of religious experience is Edwards arguing cannot be produced by argument or education alone?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Edwards's theology had instead taught that rational argument and education were fully sufficient to produce genuine faith, with no need for any additional "sense of the heart." Would a movement like the Great Awakening (which you'll study more this week) have developed the same way, or at all?
  3. Edwards was a highly educated minister trained in the same rational, argument-based theological tradition he describes as insufficient on its own. What does his own position (a learned man arguing for the limits of learning) suggest about how seriously you should take this distinction?

assignments.title: 8.2 Primary Source Exercise: Franklin on Whitefield
assignments.html:
1. Counterfactual. Franklin describes resolving not to give money, then progressively giving away his coppers, his silver, and finally his gold as Whitefield's sermon continued. Suppose Franklin had left the sermon before its conclusion. Would his account of Whitefield's persuasive skill be any less convincing to a reader today?
  2. Causation. Franklin explicitly says he remained unconvinced by "some of [Whitefield's] doctrines" while still calling him "a perfectly honest man" of clear "integrity." What does Franklin's ability to separate his judgment of Whitefield's character from his judgment of Whitefield's theology suggest about how you should evaluate historical figures whose beliefs you may not share?
  3. Concept. Edwards argues that genuine religious conviction requires a "sense of the heart," not mere rational persuasion. Franklin describes being moved, against his own prior resolution, entirely by Whitefield's oratory. Does Franklin's experience count as an example of what Edwards means by a "sense of the heart," or is it a purely rhetorical, emotional effect Edwards would consider something different entirely?
  4. Significance. Edwards writes as a believer explaining true religion from the inside; Franklin writes as a sympathetic outsider observing its effects. What can a historian learn from pairing these two very different vantage points on the same movement?

assignments.title: 9.1 Critical Questions: Rogers
assignments.html:
1. Rogers describes tactics designed to avoid ambush: varying routes, marching in dispersed single file. What do these specific, practical precautions reveal about how different frontier warfare in the Ohio Country was from the formal, close-order European battle tactics that armies like Braddock's were trained to use?
  2. Counterfactual. Rogers claims "a ranger must know the country better than his enemy, or he does not deserve the name." Suppose British commanders in this war had trained their regular soldiers in Rogers-style tactics from the beginning of the conflict. Would this have changed the war's early outcomes on the frontier?
  3. Rogers published his journals partly to build his own reputation and secure future military commissions. How might this purpose have shaped which details he chose to include and which details he might have been inclined to leave out?

assignments.title: 9.2 Primary Source Exercise: Washington's Journal

  2. Causation. Washington's own account admits the skirmish he ordered "produced consequences of a much higher nature than were foreseen by either party at that time." Why might a 22-year-old officer, writing a public account meant to justify his own conduct, choose to include this admission rather than omit it?
  3. Concept. Washington reports the French officer's blunt claim that they would hold the Ohio Country "by God" regardless of diplomatic protest. What does this exchange reveal about the actual limits of formal diplomacy when two powers both believe they have a valid claim to the same territory?
  4. Significance. This week you've read a ranger's tactical journal (Rogers) and a young officer's diplomatic-turned-military journal (Washington), both firsthand, both published to build their authors' reputations. What does comparing the two reveal about how differently a single war could be experienced depending on one's specific role within it?

assignments.title: Quarter 1 Capstone: The Contingent Colonies
assignments.html:
Overview: Over nine weeks, you have built a portfolio of fifteen primary sources spanning 1493 to 1763, from Columbus's first letter to Washington's journal of the opening skirmish of a world war. This capstone asks you to step back from any single week and make an argument about the quarter as a whole, using your own portfolio as your evidence base.

Focus Question: Of everything that happened between 1492 and 1763, what was the single most important moment where events could plausibly have gone otherwise, and what would the consequences have been if they had?

Student Directions:

  1. Choose three primary sources from your Portfolio Wall gallery, drawn from at least two different weeks, that together let you argue for a single contingent turning point across this quarter's history.
  2. Write an essay of 600–900 words, using Word headings for each of the four sections below.
  3. Section 1: The Turning Point (counterfactual). Identify your chosen turning point and argue for what would plausibly have happened differently had it gone another way. Use at least one of your three sources directly as evidence.
  4. Section 2: Causation. Explain what actually caused events to go the way they did at your turning point: a specific decision, a material condition, a piece of luck, or some combination. Use a second of your three sources.
  5. Section 3: A Figure's Virtue or Vice. Choose one historical figure connected to your turning point (Columbus, Cortés, Champlain, Smith, Bradford, Winthrop, Bacon, Whitefield, Washington, or another this quarter covered) and evaluate, in the Classical Republican sense this course uses, one specific character trait that had real explanatory power for what happened. Use your third source.
  6. Section 4: Synthesis. In 100–150 words, state directly: was your chosen turning point decided more by contingency, by a figure's character, by material conditions, or by ideas? Defend your ranking.

assignments.title: 10.1 Critical Questions: Massachusetts Body of Liberties
assignments.html:
1. The document declares that no punishment shall occur "unless it be by virtue or equity of some express law of the country." What problem is this clause trying to solve, and how does it differ from a system where a magistrate could simply decide, case by case, what seemed fair?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Massachusetts Bay's colonists had never pressed successfully for this written code, leaving magistrates free to govern entirely by their own case-by-case judgment. Would you expect the colony's government to have been more just, less just, or simply different?
  3. The Body of Liberties includes a specific protection for wives against a husband's "tyranny or cruelty." What does the inclusion of this specific, narrow protection suggest about which forms of authority the colony's leaders were and were not willing to leave entirely unregulated?
  4. This document extends "the same justice and law" to "every person within this jurisdiction, whether inhabitant or foreigner." Compare this promise to who actually held full political rights in Massachusetts Bay (Week 8). Does this document describe equal treatment before the law, equal political participation, or something narrower than either?

assignments.title: 10.2 Primary Source Report: Winthrop (Law and Magistracy)
assignments.html:
M365 Skill Step (Quarter 2 Refresher): Confirm your Optima → History → HIS7_Fall2026 OneDrive folder is still where you saved Quarter 1's work. Name your file LastName_FirstName_WinthropLawReport_HIS7. Use Heading styles for each numbered response. Submit your finished .docx by uploading it to this assignment in Canvas.

  1. Winthrop admits "there is some reason" in colonists' desire for fixed law, while still defending discretion exercised by "a few wise and godly men." Why might Winthrop feel compelled to acknowledge the other side's reasoning at all, rather than simply asserting his own authority as governor?
  2. This debate between fixed law and wise discretion is sometimes called the tension between "the rule of law" and "the rule of men." Explain, in your own words, what each phrase means, and identify which side of this debate the Massachusetts Body of Liberties ultimately came down on. In a combined 250–400 word written response covering both questions above, also address whether Winthrop's fear, that a fixed code cannot "foresee" every "particular occurrence" and might let a technicality defeat justice, has been solved once and for all by written constitutions and laws, or is a permanent, ongoing tension that any legal system, including the one you live under today, has to keep managing.

assignments.title: 11.1 Critical Questions: Dickinson
assignments.html:
1. Dickinson argues that the small size of the Townshend duties should alarm colonists rather than reassure them, since a small tax accepted now establishes a "precedent" for an unlimited tax later. Do you find this "slippery slope" reasoning persuasive as a general principle for resisting even small infringements on a right?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Parliament had instead proposed a single, one-time, very large tax rather than a small, ongoing duty. Based on Dickinson's own argument about precedent, would colonial resistance likely have been stronger, weaker, or differently motivated?
  3. Dickinson closes by urging loyalty "to the best of kings" even while making an argument that, taken to its logical end, denies Parliament's right to tax the colonies at all. What does this combination suggest about how far colonial resistance had (and had not yet) gone by 1767–68?

Note: this excerpt reproduces Dickinson's original text verbatim, including his capitalized "SLAVES," as a matter of historical accuracy to his actual 1767 argument.

assignments.title: 13.1 Critical Questions: Paul Revere's Letter
assignments.html:
1. Revere reports telling his captors "that they would be attacked before they got to Lexington" and that he had "alarmed the country all the way up." What was Revere's actual purpose in telling this to the officers who had just captured him, rather than staying silent?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Revere's ride had been intercepted before he reached anyone at all: no towns alerted, no militia warned. How might that single change have altered the battle's outcome?
  3. This account was written roughly twenty-three years after the events it describes, at another person's request. What should you keep in mind about memory and detail when evaluating a firsthand account written this long after the fact?

assignments.title: 13.2 Primary Source Exercise: The Olive Branch Petition
assignments.html:
1. Counterfactual. Suppose King George III had responded warmly to this petition. Based on what Congress had already done that same summer, do you think the fighting would have stopped, paused, or continued regardless?
  2. Causation. The petition directs its appeal specifically to the King's "royal authority," largely bypassing Parliament. Why might colonists in 1775 still have distinguished between the King and Parliament as separate targets of blame?
  3. The petition professes to be "attached to your Majesty's person, family, and government" in the same summer that Congress appointed a commander-in-chief of an army already fighting the King's troops. Is this combination best explained as sincere, strategic, or some mixture of both?
  4. Significance. King George III refused even to receive this petition formally. What does his flat rejection suggest about how much genuine possibility for reconciliation actually existed by mid-1775, regardless of how sincerely colonists hoped for it?

assignments.html:

assignments.title: 15.1 Critical Questions: Joseph Plumb Martin
assignments.html:
1. Martin writes decades after these events, as an old man reflecting on the sufferings of his youth. What details in this passage suggest a specific, vivid memory rather than a generalized, faded recollection?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Congress had reliably supplied the Continental Army with adequate food, clothing, and pay throughout the war. Do you think enlistment and desertion rates would have looked significantly different?
  3. Martin's account focuses almost entirely on cold, hunger, and physical suffering, with no mention of grand political ideas like natural rights. Does this make his account less historically valuable than the Declaration of Independence, more valuable, or valuable for a different purpose entirely?

assignments.title: 15.2 Primary Source Exercise: Cornwallis's Correspondence
assignments.html:

  2. Causation. Cornwallis describes a pattern: British forces defeat rebel forces, withdraw, and find the territory "falls again into their hands." Explain why winning individual battles failed to produce lasting territorial control.
  3. This is a private military communication, not a public document meant to persuade anyone. How might Cornwallis's willingness to admit doubt here differ from what he might have written in an official public report to London?
  4. Significance. Compare Cornwallis's frustration here to Joseph Plumb Martin's account of suffering and endurance. What do these two very different perspectives suggest about which side's soldiers and commanders more urgently needed the war to end quickly?

assignments.title: 16.2 Primary Source Exercise: Yorktown Articles of Capitulation

  3. The document insists any "doubt as to the meaning of any article" should be resolved "in the most favorable sense to the honor of the British arms." What does this reveal about how eighteenth-century military culture understood honor as something that needed protecting even in total defeat?
  4. Significance. Compare this formal document to Lafayette's warm personal letter earlier this week. What does reading a private letter between allies alongside a formal surrender document between enemies reveal about the range of relationships that all operated simultaneously during this war?

assignments.title: 17.1 Critical Questions: The Articles of Confederation
assignments.html:
1. Article II states that each state retains all power "not expressly delegated" to the national Congress. What does this specific legal default reveal about which level of government the Articles' authors trusted more?
  2. Counterfactual. Suppose Article XIII had instead required only a two-thirds vote of the states to amend the Articles, rather than unanimous consent. Do you think the Articles could have been successfully reformed rather than replaced entirely?

  3. Washington closes by openly admitting he may have "committed many errors" during his presidency. What does a departing president's public admission of possible fallibility contribute to establishing the office as a temporary, accountable public trust rather than something closer to monarchy?
  4. Significance: Semester Synthesis. assignments.title: Quarter 2 Capstone: The Contingent Republic (Fall Semester Final Project)
assignments.html:
Overview: This is the final project of the Fall semester. Over eighteen weeks and two Primary Source Portfolio Walls, you have assembled evidence spanning Columbus's first letter in 1493 to Washington's Farewell Address in 1796: the founding and survival of a specific political community, from first contact through its establishment as an independent republic. This capstone asks you to step back from any single quarter and make your strongest possible argument about the semester's full arc.

Focus Question: Of everything you have studied this Fall semester, what was the single most important contingent turning point in the whole 1492–1796 story: the moment where, had events gone differently, there might be no United States history to tell at all?

Student Directions:

  1. Choose four primary sources from your Q1 and Q2 Portfolio Walls combined, drawn from at least three different weeks and at least one source from each quarter.
  2. Write an essay of 800–1,100 words, using Word Heading 2 styles for each of the five sections below.

quizzes.title: Quarter 1 Exam: From European Exploration to the French and Indian War
quizzes.description:
Quarter 1 Exam · ~40 minutes · 27 questions

This exam covers everything from Module 1 (European exploration) through Module 9 (the French and Indian War). It does not include anything from Quarter 2. Every question requires you to connect two or more facts from across the quarter; none can be answered by recalling a single isolated sentence. Take your time.

questions.text: Portugal's King John II rejected Columbus's proposal, and Spain funded it only after a specific event completed in January 1492. Which combination of facts best explains why Spain, rather than Portugal, ended up funding the voyage that same year?

answers.text: Portugal did not believe the earth was round, while Spain did.
Portugal had already found a working sea route to Asia around Africa after Dias's 1488 voyage, while Spain's crown had just freed up its treasury and attention by completing the conquest of Granada.
Spain had no interest in reaching Asia at all.
Portugal's king died before Columbus could make his proposal.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Dias's 1488 voyage (why Portugal had no need to gamble on Columbus) with the completion of the Reconquista in January 1492 (why Spain suddenly had the resources and motive to fund him) — two separate facts from two different lessons.

questions.text: Columbus's voyage succeeded despite resting on a serious mathematical error. Which two facts, taken together, explain why the voyage was survivable anyway?

answers.text: He underestimated the distance to Asia at about 2,400 miles rather than the true 12,000, and an entire pair of continents he did not know existed happened to sit in his path.
He had more ships than any rival expedition, and his crew never doubted his judgment.
He sailed only during the safest possible season, and Spain supplied a full year of food.
He had already visited the Caribbean once before on an earlier voyage.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this the "contingent twist": two separate errors (the wrong distance estimate, and not knowing the Americas existed) had to cancel out for the voyage to work at all.

questions.text: Columbus's letter to Santángel and Hariot's Report of Virginia, written ninety-five years apart for different crowns, share an underlying purpose. What is it, and what does the gap between the two dates suggest about it?

answers.text: Both were private letters never meant to be read by anyone besides their intended recipient.
Both were written by the same author under different names.

Both belong to the genre of the promotional exploration report, written to persuade a skeptical or investing audience that a risky venture deserved continued backing, suggesting that purpose stayed constant even as the sponsoring nation and landscape changed.
Neither author had any financial or reputational stake in how the report was received.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Lesson 1.2's explicit framing of both documents as the same genre (promotional exploration report) with the specific gap in time and sponsor between them.

questions.text: Cortés landed in Mexico with roughly 600 men. Which combination of facts best explains how that force helped bring down an empire the size of the Aztec Empire?

answers.text: Tens of thousands of resentful Tlaxcalan warriors allied with Cortés against their Aztec overlords, and smallpox devastated Tenochtitlan's defenders during the final 1521 siege.
Superior Spanish cannon alone decided the outcome.
Moctezuma voluntarily abdicated before any fighting occurred.
The Spanish navy blockaded the city for over a year.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the Tlaxcalan alliance (rooted in the empire's tribute-based rule) with the separate, later fact of smallpox's toll during the siege — neither alone explains the empire's fall.

questions.text: This course's Classical Republican framework asks whether a regime binds its people into a common good or merely extracts from them by force. How does that framework help explain why Tlaxcala allied with Cortés rather than defending the Aztec Empire?

answers.text: Tlaxcala had already converted to Christianity before Cortés arrived.

The Aztec Empire ruled its subject city-states mainly through tribute extraction rather than a shared common good, so a state like Tlaxcala, bearing a long-standing grudge, had every reason to defect when a plausible ally appeared.
Tlaxcala's warriors were too weak to resist either side and had no real choice.
Cortés promised Tlaxcala full independence from any future Spanish rule.

questions.feedback_general: Requires applying the lesson's explicit Classical Republican framework (tribute without common cause breeds resentment) to the specific case of Tlaxcala's grievance.

questions.text: Díaz wrote his account of Tenochtitlan decades later as an old soldier; Cortés wrote his Second Letter to Charles V while the campaign was still underway. How does each author's specific position help explain what each source emphasizes?

answers.text: Both authors had identical purposes and produced nearly identical accounts.
Díaz wrote to secure the king's forgiveness; Cortés wrote purely for entertainment.

Díaz, writing to make sure ordinary soldiers received credit Cortés's own reports had claimed for himself alone, emphasizes the common soldiers' wonder and later loss; Cortés, needing the king's retroactive approval for an unauthorized campaign, emphasizes the city's order and profitability.
Neither author had any personal stake in how the conquest was remembered.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting each source's distinct purpose (established in each source's own "Before You Read" framing) with what each one actually chose to emphasize in the excerpt.

questions.text: Spain and France both arrived in the Americas seeking profit, yet built very different kinds of colonies. Which best explains the difference?

answers.text: France had no interest in profit, only religious conversion.

Spain found dense, resource-rich societies worth conquering and extracting from directly, while France found forests of beaver that required Native trapping skill no small French population could supply alone, pushing it toward alliance instead of conquest.
Spain's crown forbade any trade with Native peoples.
France's colonizing population outnumbered Spain's.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting what each power actually found (Spain: extractable wealth; France: furs requiring Native cooperation) with the different strategy each fact made practical.

questions.text: Unlike France's fur-trade alliances, English land settlement tended to produce lasting, persistent conflict with neighboring Native nations. Why?

answers.text: English colonists refused to trade with Native peoples under any circumstances.
France had no colonists in the Americas at all.
English settlers always outnumbered every neighboring Native nation from the moment they arrived.

A fur trade could, in principle, keep involving both parties indefinitely, while English farmland, once cleared and fenced for permanent, exclusive use, was not something its former occupants could keep sharing.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Module 3's point about a fur trade's shareable nature with its separate point about land's exclusive, permanent use once claimed for farming.

questions.text: Champlain's account of the 1609 battle is also a document a historian should read with some caution. What makes it useful evidence despite that caution?

answers.text: It should be entirely disregarded as evidence of anything.
It is useful only for details about Champlain's own religious beliefs.

Even though Champlain, who takes personal credit for the victory, should be read cautiously on his own heroism, the account still documents concretely how a new weapons technology (the arquebus) could reshape a balance of power between rival Native nations independent of any European policy.
It contains no information a historian could trust at all.

questions.feedback_general: Requires weighing the source's self-interested bias (established in the Critical Questions) against the specific kind of factual claim (weapons technology's effect) it can still support.

questions.text: Jamestown's early colonists included many gentlemen sent to search for gold, and its charter distributed food from a common store regardless of individual effort. Together, what do these two facts help explain?

answers.text: Why food production stayed dangerously low: neither the colonists' original purpose nor the incentive structure rewarded farming labor
Why the Virginia Company expected no profit at all
Why the Powhatan refused to trade with the English
Why Jamestown's site was chosen for its healthiness

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the colonists' original gold-seeking purpose with the separate incentive failure of communal food distribution, the same Classical Republican pattern the lesson names explicitly.

questions.text: Jamestown survived its earliest years largely through trade with the Powhatan Confederacy, and still suffered the devastating Starving Time. What does holding both facts together suggest about the colony's actual security?

answers.text: Jamestown was fully self-sufficient regardless of the Powhatan relationship.
The Powhatan needed Jamestown's trade goods more than Jamestown needed Powhatan corn.
Jamestown had no meaningful relationship with the Powhatan in this period.
Jamestown's survival was precarious: it depended on a neighboring power's continued goodwill even as it barely avoided starvation despite that dependence.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the colony's dependence on Powhatan trade with the separate severity of the Starving Time, rather than treating either fact as proof of security on its own.

questions.text: Tobacco farming and the fur trade you studied in Module 3 created very different long-term relationships with neighboring Native nations. Which best explains why?

answers.text: Tobacco required no land at all, unlike the fur trade.

Tobacco farming exhausted soil and demanded ever more land, creating a structural, growing English demand no diplomatic arrangement could satisfy for long, unlike a fur trade that could in principle continue indefinitely with both parties still trading.
The fur trade also demanded permanently expanding territory in the same way tobacco did.
Neither economic activity had any relationship to land use.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Module 4's tobacco economics with Module 3's fur-trade economics to see why one produced ever-escalating land conflict (culminating in the 1622 Powhatan uprising) and the other did not.

questions.text: The Mayflower landed outside the Virginia Company's chartered territory, and roughly half its passengers were not part of the original Separatist congregation that arranged the voyage. Together, what did these two facts make especially necessary?

answers.text: A new religious congregation with different beliefs
A renegotiation of the loan from the Merchant Adventurers
A new civil agreement establishing shared authority, since neither an existing charter nor a shared prior loyalty could be assumed to bind everyone aboard
An immediate return voyage to England before winter

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the jurisdictional gap with the separate fact that half the passengers had no prior tie to the original congregation, since either fact alone would leave a weaker case for why the Mayflower Compact was necessary.

questions.text: Tisquantum and Massasoit both helped Plymouth survive its first year, but in different capacities. Which best distinguishes their two contributions?

answers.text: Tisquantum commanded Wampanoag warriors in battle; Massasoit taught the colonists English.
Tisquantum provided translation and practical advice; Massasoit concluded a mutual-defense treaty with the colony.
Both served purely as religious advisors to the Separatist congregation.
Massasoit was a Merchant Adventurer investor; Tisquantum was a Plymouth colonist.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Tisquantum's specific role (language and advice) with Massasoit's separate, different role (treaty diplomacy).

questions.text: Jamestown and Plymouth both began with communal farming, both saw production stay low, and both eventually assigned private plots to individual families. What does this repeated pattern, across two colonies founded by different religious groups thirteen years apart, suggest?

answers.text: The repetition across two independent colonies under different charters is a pattern serious enough that a historian should take the underlying incentive explanation seriously, not dismiss it as chance.
It is most likely a coincidence with no broader explanatory value.
It proves that all seventeenth-century English colonies used the exact same charter.
It shows that Plymouth copied Jamestown's official government structure exactly.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Module 4's Jamestown incentive failure with Module 5's explicit statement that Plymouth repeated "almost the exact same mistake," treating the cross-week repetition itself as evidence.

questions.text: Which combination of facts best explains why New England developed dense, town-centered settlement while the South developed dispersed plantations?

answers.text: New England colonists distrusted city life while Southern planters did not.
New England had far more available land than the South.
Southern cash crops required no land at all.
New England land was granted to groups of settlers together for town-centered farming, while Southern cash crops like tobacco required large, spread-out landholdings to grow profitably.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting New England's group-land-grant pattern with the South's separate cash-crop land demands, the same material-conditions logic the lesson explicitly compares to Module 3's great-powers strategies.

questions.text: New York and Pennsylvania each became unusually diverse for English America, but for different specific reasons. Which best distinguishes them?

answers.text: New York inherited a mixed population from its earlier existence as the Dutch colony of New Netherland; Pennsylvania's founder William Penn actively recruited settlers of many faiths, including Quakers, Germans, and Scots-Irish.
Both colonies became diverse purely by accident, for identical and unknown reasons.
New York recruited its diversity deliberately; Pennsylvania inherited it from a prior colonial power.
Neither colony was more diverse than New England.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting New York's distinct historical cause (Dutch inheritance) with Pennsylvania's distinct historical cause (Penn's deliberate recruitment), rather than treating "diversity" as a single undifferentiated fact.

questions.text: Bacon's Rebellion burned Jamestown to the ground in September 1676, yet collapsed within weeks. What does the timing of its collapse suggest?

answers.text: Royal forces had already defeated Bacon in open battle before his death.

Bacon's sudden death from dysentery, only weeks after burning Jamestown, effectively ended the rebellion, suggesting the coalition's cohesion depended heavily on Bacon personally rather than on a shared program that could survive without him.
The rebellion had already achieved all its stated goals before Bacon died.

quizzes.title: Quarter 2 Exam: From Colonial Self-Government to Washington's Presidency
quizzes.description:
Quarter 2 Exam · ~40 minutes · 27 questions

This exam covers everything from Module 10 (colonial self-government) through Module 18 (Washington's presidency and the Fall semester's close). It does not include anything from Quarter 1. Every question requires you to connect two or more facts from across the quarter; none can be answered by recalling a single isolated sentence. Take your time.

questions.text: English colonial charters varied enormously (royal, joint-stock, proprietary), yet nearly all colonies ended up sharing one feature regardless of charter type. What was it?

answers.text: Complete independence from any crown authority.
A ban on all forms of local elections.
An elected assembly giving property-holding male colonists a voice in local law, even though the colony still ultimately answered to the crown.
Identical written constitutions in every colony.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the fact that charter types differed widely with the separate fact that colonies converged on the same outcome despite that variety, rather than treating charter type as the whole story.

questions.text: A Massachusetts Bay resident who could never vote for the colony's governor might still vote directly on his own town's budget every year. Which two facts together explain this apparent contradiction?

answers.text: Only church members were allowed to live in New England towns at all.
Colony-wide elections restricted voting to full church members, while town meetings extended direct participation to all property-holding male residents regardless of religious status.
Town meetings and colony-wide elections used identical eligibility rules.
Governors were elected directly by town meetings.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the colony-wide voting restriction (church membership) with the separate, broader town-meeting eligibility rule to explain the apparent contradiction.

questions.text: John Winthrop favored magistrate discretion, while other colonists pushed for the fixed, written Massachusetts Body of Liberties. What was actually at stake in that disagreement?

answers.text: Whether Massachusetts Bay should have any government at all.
Whether the colony should remain loyal to the English crown.
Whether town meetings should be abolished entirely.

Whether a wise magistrate's case-by-case judgment or a predictable, written code that applied equally to everyone should govern the colony, a tension the course tracks all the way to the Constitutional Convention.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Winthrop's specific argument for discretion with the colonists' specific argument for a fixed code, recognizing this as the same discretion-versus-fixed-law tension the course revisits later at the Convention.

questions.text: The Proclamation of 1763 was intended to reduce conflict with Native nations after Pontiac's Rebellion, yet it became deeply unpopular among colonists, including land speculators like George Washington. Why did a measure meant to prevent conflict provoke colonial anger instead?

answers.text: Colonists believed the war's victory should have opened western land for their own settlement and speculation, so a measure blocking that land felt like a betrayal of what the victory was supposed to deliver.
The Proclamation actually gave colonists more land than they had before the war.
George Washington personally supported the Proclamation.
Pontiac's Rebellion had nothing to do with the Proclamation's timing.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the Proclamation's stated defensive purpose with the separate fact of colonists' and speculators' expectations from the war's victory.

questions.text: Colonial protest against the Sugar Act (1764) was real but limited, while the Stamp Act (1765) provoked organized boycotts, a congress, and direct intimidation of officials. What best explains this difference in reaction?

answers.text: The Sugar Act applied only to Massachusetts, while the Stamp Act applied everywhere.
The Stamp Act raised no real revenue.
Colonists had no objection to either act on principle.
The Sugar Act actually lowered the existing molasses tax even while tightening enforcement, while the Stamp Act was a new direct tax applied without any colonial assembly's consent.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the Sugar Act's rate-cut-but-stricter-enforcement combination with the Stamp Act's status as a new, consent-free direct tax.

questions.text: Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 partly because British merchants were losing business to colonial boycotts. Which fact about what Parliament did at the same time shows this was a tactical retreat rather than a genuine concession?

answers.text: Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act, asserting its right to tax and legislate for the colonies "in all cases whatsoever."
Parliament simultaneously granted the colonies permanent representation in the House of Commons.
Parliament simultaneously abolished all future taxation of the colonies.
Parliament simultaneously extended the Proclamation Line further west.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the merchant-pressure reason for repeal with the separate fact of what Parliament asserted at the same moment.

questions.text: Parliament kept the tax on tea specifically to preserve the principle that it could tax the colonies, then passed the Tea Act to make taxed tea cheaper than smuggled tea. Why did colonial leaders treat the cheaper tea as more dangerous, not less?

answers.text: Buying the now-affordable taxed tea would mean tacitly accepting the very taxing principle Parliament had deliberately preserved, undermining years of resistance in a single purchase.
The tea itself was reportedly poisoned.
Cheaper tea meant colonial merchants would lose all profit from tea sales.
Parliament secretly planned to raise the tea tax again immediately.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Parliament's reason for keeping the tea tax with the separate mechanism of the Tea Act's price cut, to see why cheaper tea was exactly the trap.

questions.text: Contemporary accounts describe the Boston Tea Party as orderly, with no other property damaged and the decks swept clean afterward. Why does this specific discipline matter for how a historian should read this period's primary sources?

answers.text: It shows the participants had no real political motive at all.
Organizers likely wanted their protest to look controlled and lawful, supporting their claim to be defending constitutional rights rather than acting as a violent mob.
It proves the British government secretly organized the event.
It shows the tea was worthless and not worth guarding.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the specific factual details of the event's orderliness with the interpretive point about why that discipline mattered to how the protest would be perceived.

questions.text: Parliament designed the Intolerable (Coercive) Acts to isolate and punish Massachusetts alone. Why did this strategy fail?

answers.text: Massachusetts refused all outside help.
Britain repealed the Acts before any other colony could respond.

Other colonies, recognizing that a Parliament willing to gut one colony's charter and self-government could do the same to any of them next, sent aid and solidarity to Massachusetts at real cost to themselves.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Parliament's isolating strategy with the separate fact of how other colonies actually responded, recognizing shared fear and years of prior grievance as the reason the strategy backfired.

questions.text: The Boston Pamphlet did not spread to other towns on its own. Which organization, built by Samuel Adams, provided the network that circulated documents like it across Massachusetts and beyond?

answers.text: The Second Continental Congress.

questions.text: John Adams and his cousin Samuel Adams both resisted British policy, but in different ways. Which best distinguishes their two approaches?

answers.text: John worked mainly through formal legal argument (as in his Boston Massacre defense); Samuel worked through organizing, persuasion, and inflammatory political framing (as in the Committees of Correspondence).

questions.text: In the summer of 1775, the Second Continental Congress appointed Washington commander of the new Continental Army and approved the Olive Branch Petition to King George III. Why are these two acts not contradictory?

answers.text: Congress secretly intended the petition to fail from the start.

They reflected where most delegates' actual thinking stood: prepared to defend colonial rights by force if necessary, while still sincerely hoping reconciliation with the king remained possible.

questions.text: Common Sense was published in January 1776, just as news of the Olive Branch Petition's rejection was becoming widely known. Why did this timing matter for the pamphlet's impact?

answers.text: Colonists who had just watched their loyal appeal for reconciliation fail were primed to hear Paine's case that reconciliation with the monarchy itself was the wrong goal to begin with.
The timing was coincidental and had no real effect on the pamphlet's reception.
Paine wrote the pamphlet in direct response to Washington's appointment.
The Olive Branch Petition's rejection was caused by Common Sense's publication.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the specific publication timing with the separate content of what Paine actually argued, rather than treating the timing as incidental.

questions.text: How did Thomas Paine's argument in Common Sense go further than John Dickinson's Letters from a Pennsylvania Farmer or the Olive Branch Petition?

answers.text: Paine argued for continued loyalty to the crown.
Paine made no argument about government at all.

Paine argued against hereditary monarchy as a system of government, not just against particular royal or parliamentary policies, unlike the earlier documents' continued profession of loyalty to the crown.
Paine argued only against Parliament, exactly as Dickinson had.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting what Dickinson's and the Olive Branch Petition's arguments actually accepted with the separate fact of what Paine specifically rejected.

questions.text: The Declaration of Independence blames King George III personally and specifically, almost entirely omitting Parliament, even though parliamentary taxes and acts had been the primary source of colonial grievance for over a decade. Why might the drafters have made this specific rhetorical choice?

answers.text: Parliament had no involvement in any colonial policy at all.

The Declaration's Lockean argument holds that a government forfeits legitimate authority when it becomes destructive of natural rights, and that argument needed an identifiable party who had done the forfeiting, a shift Common Sense had already begun.
The King had no actual power over colonial policy, so blaming him was arbitrary.
The drafters forgot to mention Parliament by accident.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the Declaration's Lockean theoretical structure with the separate, deliberate rhetorical choice to personalize blame, and with Common Sense's earlier shift away from blaming Parliament.

questions.text: Washington's core insight was that his army needed to survive and endure rather than win decisive battles outright. Which combination of facts best explains why this strategy suited the Continental Army's actual situation?

answers.text: The Continental Army had more soldiers than Britain from the very start of the war.
Washington believed a single decisive battle would end the war quickly in America's favor.
Britain had no navy and could not resupply its army at all.

Britain's professional army and powerful navy made head-on decisive victory unlikely, while a prolonged war of endurance would impose costs Britain, fighting far from home, would eventually have to weigh against the war's value.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Britain's specific listed advantages with Washington's specific strategic response, rather than treating the strategy as an unexplained preference.

questions.text: Why did the timing of the Trenton and Princeton victories in the winter of 1776–77 matter so much, despite their small military scale?

answers.text: They were the largest battles of the entire war.
They occurred just as most Continental Army enlistments were about to expire and morale had collapsed, reviving flagging confidence at the precise moment both were about to collapse entirely.
They ended the war immediately.
They occurred years after the crisis they are usually credited with resolving.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the small military scale of these battles with the separate, looming administrative deadline of expiring enlistments.

questions.text: Unlike the thirteen rebelling colonies, East and West Florida remained firmly loyal to the British crown throughout the Revolution. Why does this matter for how a student should think about "the colonies" during the war?

answers.text: It shows Florida had no British colonial history at all before the Revolution.
It proves every colony eventually joined the Revolution by 1781.

It shows the Revolution was, among other things, a civil conflict within British America, not simply "the colonies versus Britain," since Florida and significant Loyalist populations elsewhere actively opposed the rebellion.
It shows Spain controlled Florida throughout the entire war.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting Florida's specific Loyalist status with the lesson's explicit warning against treating "the colonies" as a single unified bloc.

questions.text: France had already been secretly supplying money and weapons to the Americans for two years before the Battle of Saratoga (1777). What did Saratoga actually change?

answers.text: It was the first moment France had any involvement with the American cause at all.
It ended France's interest in the war entirely.
It caused France to break off all support until after the battle.
It convinced France that open, formal alliance was now a realistic bet rather than a reckless gamble, not that France should begin helping America for the first time.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the earlier fact of two years of secret French aid with the separate fact of what Saratoga specifically triggered.

questions.text: What combination of motives explains France's 1778 decision to formally ally with the United States?

answers.text: Purely idealistic sympathy with no strategic interest at all.
A mix of genuine Enlightenment sympathy for the American cause among some French officials and a colder strategic calculation about weakening Britain, France's chief global rival.
Purely financial profit with no political motive.
A direct request from King George III.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting genuine sympathy among French officials with the separate, colder strategic calculation about Britain, rather than treating either motive alone as the whole explanation.

questions.text: The naval Battle of the Chesapeake (September 1781) was fought entirely between French and British fleets, with no Continental Army soldier involved. Why did this naval battle decide the outcome of the land siege at Yorktown?

answers.text: The naval battle and the land siege were entirely unconnected events that happened to occur around the same time.
Cornwallis's surrender resulted from a separate land battle that defeated his army decisively.
The French fleet's victory secured control of the bay and sealed off Cornwallis's only escape or resupply route by sea, making his position untenable regardless of how his land forces performed.
The French navy directly attacked Yorktown's land fortifications.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the naval outcome (control of the bay) with the separate strategic consequence for Cornwallis's land position (no resupply, no retreat), rather than treating the two as unrelated events.

questions.text: Congress under the Articles of Confederation could only request funds from state legislatures, which frequently ignored those requests. Which separate weakness of the Articles meant Congress had no way to compel payment when states refused?

answers.text: Congress had no independent executive branch or national judiciary to enforce its own requests or laws.
Congress had unlimited power to tax citizens directly instead.
States were legally forbidden from ever refusing a congressional request.
The Articles required only a simple majority to amend, making enforcement easy.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the funding-request weakness with the separate structural fact that Congress had no executive or judiciary to enforce anything.

questions.text: Shays' Rebellion (1786–87) was ultimately suppressed by force. Which combination of facts explains whose force that was, and why?

answers.text: The national Congress raised a federal army to suppress the rebellion directly.
No force of any kind was used to end the rebellion.
Massachusetts's own state militia suppressed the uprising, because the national Congress under the Articles had neither the funds nor the legal authority to raise a federal force to respond.
British troops still stationed in America intervened.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the fact of state-level suppression with the separate fact of the national government's specific incapacity, rather than assuming any single government body handled it.

questions.text: The Constitutional Convention resolved two separate, serious conflicts: large states versus small states, and slave states versus free states over how enslaved people would count toward population. Which two compromises, respectively, resolved them?

answers.text: Both conflicts were resolved by the single Three-Fifths Compromise alone.

The Great (Connecticut) Compromise created a bicameral legislature to resolve the large-state/small-state conflict; the Three-Fifths Compromise resolved the representation-and-taxation conflict over enslaved population.
The Great Compromise addressed slavery, while the Three-Fifths Compromise addressed state representation.
Neither conflict was actually resolved at the Convention.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting each of the two distinct conflicts with its own distinct, separately named resolution, rather than collapsing the Convention's work into a single compromise.

questions.text: Anti-Federalists raised two distinct objections to the Constitution: that it concentrated dangerous federal power, and that it lacked a bill of rights. Which of these two objections did the eventual ratification compromise directly address?

answers.text: Both objections were fully resolved by eliminating the federal government's new powers.
Neither objection was ever addressed in any way.
The bill-of-rights objection, through a pledge to add rights-protecting amendments, not the broader concentrated-power objection.
The concentrated-power objection alone, by returning to the Articles of Confederation.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the two distinct Anti-Federalist objections with the specific compromise that followed, to see which one was actually addressed.

questions.text: Nothing in the Constitution required George Washington to leave office after two terms, yet he did so voluntarily in 1796. Why does this specific choice matter as much as this course's Classical Republican framework suggests?

answers.text: It established an unwritten norm, followed for a century and a half, demonstrating that the presidency was a temporary public trust rather than a permanent personal possession, a stable act of self-restraint with real explanatory value for the republic's survival.
It had no lasting effect on how future presidents behaved.
It was required by an amendment already in place at the time.
It reflected Washington's declining personal popularity, which made re-election impossible.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the fact that this norm was voluntary and unenforced with the framework's specific emphasis on stable character traits, like self-restraint, that have genuine explanatory value for a regime's success.

questions.text: Washington's Farewell Address warned against the "baneful effects of the spirit of party." Which specific development within his own presidency does this warning most directly connect to?

answers.text: A foreign invasion Washington feared during his presidency.
A dispute over the location of the new national capital.
The Bill of Rights ratification process of 1791.
The emerging Hamilton-Jefferson split within his own Cabinet over federal financial policy, an early sign of the organized political parties Washington explicitly hoped to prevent.

questions.feedback_general: Requires connecting the Farewell Address's specific warning with the earlier lesson's account of the Hamilton-Jefferson Cabinet disagreement that first revealed this danger.
