questions.text: Free response.

Across eighteen weeks, this course has asked you to evaluate historical figures by specific character traits with real explanatory power, not by simple praise or blame. Looking back across the whole Fall semester, name the single virtue or vice you now think best explains how this specific political community managed to come into existence at all, and defend your choice.

discussions.title: 1.2 Discussion: Voyage of Columbus
discussions.html: State one specific claim about why Columbus succeeded in reaching land alive in 1492 when his proposal had been rejected for years before that, and explain what evidence from this week's lesson supports your claim. Then reply to one classmate: does their explanation rely more on Columbus's own persistence and character, or on circumstances outside his control (the Reconquista's completion, the errors in his math, the accident of an intervening continent)? Which explanation do you find more convincing, and why?

discussions.title: 2.2 Discussion: Cortés' Conquest of Mexico
discussions.html: State one specific claim about the single most important contingent factor in the Spanish victory over the Aztec Empire (Tlaxcalan alliances, smallpox, Malintzin's translation, or Cortés's own decisions) and defend it with evidence. Then reply to a classmate: does their chosen factor complement yours, or compete with it? Could both be "the most important" at once, or does picking one require ranking it above the others?

discussions.title: 3.2 Discussion: France, Indians, and the Fur Trade
discussions.html: State one specific claim about whether France's fur-trade alliance model or England's land-settlement model (which you'll study starting next week) was more likely to lead to long-term conflict with Native nations, and defend it using this week's evidence. Then reply to a classmate, testing their claim against the counterexample of the Beaver Wars, a case where alliance-based trade still produced decades of warfare.

discussions.title: 4.2 Discussion: The Anglo-Powhatan Wars
discussions.html: State one specific claim about what mattered most in turning Anglo-Powhatan relations from uneasy peace to open war: the death of Powhatan and Pocahontas's marriage, the structural land demands of tobacco farming, or some third factor. Defend your claim with specific evidence. Then reply to a classmate: does their explanation treat 1622 as inevitable, or as one contingent outcome among several that might have happened instead?

discussions.title: 5.2 Discussion: Pilgrims at Plymouth Rock
discussions.html: State one specific claim about what mattered most to Plymouth's survival through its first two years: the Mayflower Compact's self-government, aid and diplomacy from the Wampanoag, or the 1623 shift to private farming plots. Defend your claim. Then reply to a classmate: could their chosen factor have succeeded on its own, without the other two also being present?

discussions.title: 6.2 Discussion: The Virginia Company and Bacon's Rebellion
discussions.html: State one specific claim about whether Bacon's Rebellion should be understood mainly as a conflict over Native American policy, a conflict over elite corruption and trade monopolies, or a combination that cannot be neatly separated. Defend your claim with specific evidence from the Declaration. Then reply to a classmate: does separating these causes clarify the event, or does it distort a grievance that Bacon's own followers experienced as one connected complaint?

discussions.title: 7.2 Discussion: Slave Trade in Africa, incl. Arab and Barbary Pirates
discussions.html: State one specific claim about what made the Atlantic slave trade distinct from the slave-trading systems (trans-Saharan, Indian Ocean, Barbary) that predated it, and defend it with evidence from both lessons. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer emphasize scale, permanence of status, racial categorization, or something else, and is that the most important distinction, in your view?

discussions.title: 8.2 Discussion: Whitefield, Edwards, and the Great Awakenings
discussions.html: State one specific claim about whether the Great Awakening represented a betrayal of Massachusetts Bay's founding Puritan vision or its logical continuation a century later, and defend it with evidence from this week's lessons and sources. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer treat "Old Light" clergy as the true heirs of the founders, or "New Light" revivalists as the true heirs, and could both sides have a legitimate claim?

discussions.title: 9.2 Discussion: The Disputed Ohio Country
discussions.html: State one specific claim about which party (France, Virginia and its land speculators, or the Ohio Country's Native nations) had the most legitimate claim to the territory in the 1750s, and defend it. Then reply to a classmate: does their argument rest on prior occupation, legal charter, military capacity, or some other standard of legitimacy, and is that standard one you would apply consistently to all three parties?

discussions.title: 10.2 Discussion: The New England Town Hall
discussions.html: State one specific claim about whether the New England town meeting or the Massachusetts Body of Liberties did more to build lasting habits of American self-government, and defend it. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer distinguish between a practice (participating in a meeting) and a text (a written code of rights) as two different kinds of civic education?

discussions.title: 11.2 Discussion: The Sugar and Stamp Acts and the Boston Massacre
discussions.html: State one specific claim about which single British policy between 1763 and 1770 (the Proclamation Line, the Stamp Act, or the Townshend Acts' funding of royal officials) did the most to convince colonists that Parliament posed a genuine threat to their self-government. Then reply to a classmate: does their chosen policy threaten colonists' wallets, their assemblies' power, or their sense of consent and representation most directly?

discussions.title: 12.2 Discussion: The Intolerable Acts
discussions.html: State one specific claim about why Parliament's strategy of isolating and punishing Massachusetts alone failed to work by 1774, and defend it with evidence. Then reply to a classmate: does their explanation rest mainly on shared colonial ideas, shared colonial fear, or organized colonial action, and which of the three do you think mattered most?

discussions.title: 13.2 Discussion: Boston and Samuel Adams
discussions.html: State one specific claim comparing the views of committed Patriots, committed Loyalists, and colonists still hoping for reconciliation in the summer of 1775 on the question of resistance to British authority. Then reply to a classmate: does their comparison suggest any one of the three positions was more internally consistent than the others?

discussions.title: 14.2 Discussion: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson
discussions.html: State one specific claim about why Adams's choice to let Jefferson draft the Declaration, rather than writing it himself, mattered to the document's success in uniting colonial opinion. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer emphasize Jefferson's writing skill, Adams's political liabilities, or something else?

discussions.title: 15.2 Discussion: The Continental Congress
discussions.html: State one specific claim about what the Continental Congress most urgently needed to provide the Continental Army during the crisis of winter 1776–77 (money, supplies, political unity, or something else) and defend it. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer treat Congress's failures as a cause of the army's suffering, or as an unavoidable limitation?

discussions.title: 16.2 Discussion: The French Connection
discussions.html: State one specific claim about whether the American Revolution could plausibly have succeeded without French intervention and defend it with evidence from this quarter. Then reply to a classmate: does their answer treat French support as necessary for victory, merely helpful in speeding it up, or something in between?

discussions.title: 17.2 Discussion: James Madison and Alexander Hamilton
discussions.html: State one specific claim about which single change from the Articles of Confederation to the Constitution mattered most for fixing the weaknesses Shays' Rebellion exposed (direct taxation power, an executive branch, or the easier amendment process) and defend it. Then reply to a classmate: does their chosen change address the specific problem Shays' Rebellion revealed, or a different problem entirely?

discussions.title: 18.2 Discussion: George Washington
discussions.html: State one specific claim about which of Washington's choices (accepting the unanimous 1789 election, forming a Cabinet with genuinely opposed views, or voluntarily stepping down after two terms) mattered most for the survival of the young republic. Then reply to a classmate: does their chosen decision address a first-order political problem this course's framework has tracked all semester, or a different kind of problem?
